The evidence explicitly states in the notes and code comments that 'If the loop terminates before reaching the final cell (x1, y1), explicitly visit (x1, y1) to ensure the end cell is included.' The subsequent check `if (currentX != x1 || currentY != y1) { visitor.visit(x1, y1); }` (lines 113-115 in the float version, implied by the notes for the fixed-point versions) confirms that the loop may terminate before visiting the final cell, necessitating the explicit inclusion. Thus, the claim that the loop condition may terminate before the final cell is visited is supported by the evidence.

This is computed as the absolute distance to the next boundary multiplied by the inverse step size, then right-shifted to normalize [S1, unofficial].

The claim describes the computation of `tMax` (or `tMaxX_fp`/`tMaxY_fp`) in the Amanatides-Woo algorithm implementation. Specifically, it states: 'absolute distance to the next boundary multiplied by the inverse step size, then right-shifted to normalize'. Looking at the evidence in Source [S1], specifically lines 247-248 for the 32-bit fixed-point implementation: `fl::abs(fl::i64(nextX_fp - startX_fp)) * absDeltaX_fp >> FP_SHIFT`. Here, `nextX_fp - startX_fp` is the distance to the next boundary, `absDeltaX_fp` is the inverse step size (delta T per unit distance, effectively), and `>> FP_SHIFT` is the right-shift to normalize the fixed-point result. This matches the claim exactly.
